title: The Two Ways: The Tree and the Chaff
summary: The first psalm blesses the person who refuses the company and counsel of the wicked and instead delights in the law of the LORD, meditating on it day and night. Such a person is like a tree planted by streams of water, fruitful and flourishing. The wicked are like chaff blown away by the wind; they will not stand in the judgment, for the LORD watches over the way of the righteous, while the way of the wicked perishes.
story: Psalm 1 is the front door of the Psalter. It has no heading and no named author, and it doesn't address God at all; it speaks to the reader. That is fitting for an introduction. Before the book offers 149 other psalms of praise, lament, and thanks, it tells the reader what kind of person will pray them well: one whose life is shaped by God's instruction. The psalm's two ways, the path of the righteous and the way of the wicked, set the terms for much of what follows. Again and again the later psalms will wrestle with the prosperity of the wicked and the suffering of the righteous, and Psalm 1's confidence will be tested hard. Psalm 2, which follows, adds the second great theme of the introduction: God's king on Zion.
historical:
Psalm 1 carries no superscription, and nothing in it ties it to a specific event or reign. Most scholars classify it as a wisdom psalm or a torah psalm (with Psalms 19 and 119), and many think it was written or chosen by the editors who arranged the Psalter, to serve as its preface. On that view it would belong to the later stages of the collection's formation, perhaps in the Persian period after the exile, when devotion to the written law became central to Jewish life. Others argue that its language and themes could come from earlier wisdom circles in the monarchy, and that its placement at the head of the book, not its date of writing, is what marks it as an introduction.

Psalms 1 and 2 were closely linked in antiquity. Psalm 1 opens with blessed and Psalm 2 ends with blessed, framing the two as a pair. Some ancient Jewish tradition treated them as a single psalm, and a few early manuscripts of Acts 13:33 quote Psalm 2 as the first psalm. The image of the tree by water closely resembles Jeremiah 17:7-8, and scholars debate whether one text borrowed from the other or both drew on a shared tradition.
cultural:
The tree in verse 3 is not a tree that happens to grow by a river. The verb means transplanted, set out deliberately, and the streams of water are channels or canals, the irrigation ditches that farmers dug to bring water to orchards. In the dry climate of the ancient Near East, where rain was seasonal and summers were long and parched, a tree planted beside a channel had a constant water supply and stayed green when others withered. The picture is of a life deliberately rooted near a reliable source.

The chaff in verse 4 comes from the threshing floor. After harvest, farmers beat or trampled the grain, then tossed it into the air with a winnowing fork on a windy day. The heavy grain fell back to the floor, and the light husks blew away. Every ancient reader had seen this, and the image makes a pointed contrast: the tree is rooted and heavy with fruit, while the chaff has no weight and no root. The assembly of the righteous (verse 5) may recall the gathering of the community at the city gate or before God, and some read the judgment here as God's final verdict.
literary: The psalm is built on contrast. Verses 1 to 3 describe the righteous person; verses 4 and 5 describe the wicked; verse 6 gives the reason for the difference. Verse 1 has a descending progression of three verbs and three nouns: walking in the counsel of the wicked, standing on the path of sinners, sitting in the seat of mockers. The movement from walking to standing to sitting suggests how drift into evil becomes settled. Verse 2 turns on the word “But” and gives the positive alternative in two lines about the law. The abrupt “Not so the wicked” opens the second half. The psalm begins with “Blessed” and ends with “perish”, the first and last words of the Hebrew text marking the two destinies.

outline.t: The blessed person, rooted in God's instruction
The wicked, like chaff before the wind
The LORD watches over the way of the righteous

doctrines.note: The psalm teaches that life has two ways and that the choice between them is shown by what a person delights in and meditates on. Wisdom here is not cleverness but a life shaped by God's instruction.

The law of the LORD, God's instruction, is presented as a gift to delight in and meditate on. By placing this psalm first, the editors present the whole Psalter as instruction to be absorbed, not just songs to be sung.

The wicked will not stand in the judgment, and their way will perish. The psalm is confident that God distinguishes between the righteous and the wicked, even when, as many later psalms admit, that distinction is not yet visible.

words.note: Esher, blessed or happy, from the phrase ashre ha-ish, blessed is the man. The word describes a state of flourishing, the good life as God intends it, rather than a feeling or a pronouncement of blessing by God. It opens the Psalter and returns often in it, and Jesus' beatitudes use the same form (Matthew 5:3-11).

Torah, usually translated law but more broadly meaning instruction or teaching. It can refer to the law of Moses, to the first five books of the Bible, or to God's teaching in general. Here it is something to delight in, not a burden, and some think Psalm 1 invites the reader to treat the Psalter itself as torah.

Hagah, translated meditate, but its basic sense is to murmur or mutter. Ancient reading was usually aloud, and meditation meant repeating a text under one's breath until it sank in. The same verb appears in Psalm 2:1, where the peoples plot or mutter in vain, a deliberate contrast between the two psalms.

Yada, to know. Verse 6 literally says the LORD knows the way of the righteous; the BSB renders it guards. In Hebrew, to know often means to be in close relationship with and to care for. The righteous way is known by God, while the way of the wicked perishes.

christ: Psalm 1 describes an ideal: a person wholly shaped by God's word, never walking in the counsel of the wicked, always fruitful. Israel's own history, recorded in the psalms that follow, shows how rarely anyone lived up to it. Christians have long recognized Jesus as the one who fulfilled this picture completely; some early Christian interpreters, Augustine among them, read the blessed man of Psalm 1 as Christ himself. This reading is best understood as fulfillment rather than prediction: the psalm describes the righteous life, and the Gospels show the one who lived it. Jesus answered temptation with Scripture (Matthew 4:1-11), called his followers blessed in the Beatitudes, and used the image of the tree and its fruit (Matthew 7:17-20). For Christians, the way of the righteous is found by union with the one who walked it perfectly.

hard.q: Does Psalm 1 promise that righteous people will always prosper?
hard.a:
Verse 3 says the righteous person prospers in all he does, and a surface reading could suggest a guarantee of success. But the Psalter itself refuses that reading. Psalm 73 describes a righteous man envying the prosperity of the wicked, and many laments complain that the righteous suffer while the wicked flourish. The book of Job argues the same point at length.

Interpreters have read Psalm 1 in several ways. Some take its promises as a general principle of wisdom, true over the long run but not in every case, much like the proverbs. Others read the prospering as spiritual flourishing, the fruitfulness of a life rooted in God, which may coexist with outward loss. Still others read verses 5 and 6 as pointing to the final judgment, when the difference between the two ways will be fully revealed. What the psalm doesn't do is promise that faithfulness will be rewarded on a human timetable; the tree yields its fruit in season, not on demand.

questions: The psalm moves from walking to standing to sitting with the wicked. Where have you seen small compromises become settled habits?
The tree is deliberately planted by streams of water. What practices keep you rooted near a reliable source when life is dry?
Psalm 1 says the righteous will prosper, yet later psalms complain that the wicked flourish. How do you hold these together?
